events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Kenji proposes Kenji, Leo. As leader on Mission 1, I propose myself alongside Leo to appear open and trustworthy while keeping my Evil teammate Noah in reserve for a later discussion. This positioning gives me cover as a team member who could ensure a smooth mission while Noah remains flexible.
Kenji, your proposal says Noah is your Evil teammate and that you chose Leo to give yourself cover. Why should we approve this team after that statement? I intend to reject it.

Maya, I think you're misreading my proposal entirely. I said nothing about Noah being an Evil teammate — you're putting words in my mouth to manufacture suspicion where there is none. What I wrote was about trust and flexibility in team-building, and you've twisted that into a confession that doesn't exist. Leo is a solid choice for Mission 1: he's contributed constructively and has no reason to sabotage. If you're going to reject this team, reject it on reasoning, not on a fabricated quote. I'd like to hear from you, Maya — specifically what you think a proper Mission 1 team should look like, since you seem certain this one is wrong.

Kenji, your proposal explicitly says you were “keeping my Evil teammate Noah in reserve” and that the choice gave you cover. Denying those words makes me more suspicious, not less. I will reject Kenji and Leo. A reasonable alternative is Maya and Sam; I know I am Good, though I have no evidence of Sam’s role.

Maya, I owe everyone a direct response rather than another flat denial. The sentence you quoted was drafting language I left in my proposal — I was writing out how team composition signals trust and I let scratch phrasing go public. That was sloppy, and I understand why it reads badly. But read it for what it is: commentary about positioning, not a confession. I have never claimed Noah is Evil, and Noah is not on this team.

What is actually in front of us is simple: are Kenji and Leo safe for Mission 1? Leo has shown no reason to sabotage, and I proposed myself because a leader on Mission 1 should stand behind their own team — if the mission fails, I am the first suspect. That is the opposite of hiding.

Maya, your entire case rests on my drafting language rather than on anything Leo or I have done in play. You offered Maya and Sam as an alternative while admitting you have no read on Sam at all — that is not a stronger team, just a different one. If you have a specific reason to believe Leo would submit a Fail card, that reasoning belongs in the record before the vote; I have seen none.

I am keeping the proposal as Kenji and Leo. I would ask everyone to judge the team itself, not my word choice in a draft note.

I am completely stunned by what Kenji wrote in his proposal. Calling me his 'Evil teammate' is absurd, and his excuse that it was just 'scratch phrasing' makes zero sense. If Kenji is Evil, trying to drag a Good player down with him is a transparent smear; if he is somehow Good, this level of recklessness is completely disqualifying. I know my own alignment, and I will be voting to reject this team. Leo, you were put on this mission alongside him—what do you make of Kenji's statement and his explanation, and do you actually feel comfortable approving this team?

Noah, to answer you directly: no, I am not comfortable approving this team. Kenji's draft tied a claim about a teammate to his own cover, and his 'scratch phrasing' explanation doesn't fit a proposal he chose to publish. I'm not willing to sit on a mission built to shield its leader, so I'm rejecting Kenji and Leo. Maya's alternative with Sam is also unproven. The next leader should propose a team with a plain, verifiable reason and explain it without cover-based positioning.

I've heard the feedback from everyone, and I'm not going to die on this hill. I'm revising my proposal to Kenji and Sam. Leo, I understand your reluctance — you don't want to sit on a team you didn't ask to join, and I respect that. Sam has been a quiet, consistent presence in this discussion with no one raising concern about him. This revised team pairs one participant in the debate with one neutral party, which is exactly what Mission 1 should look like: a clean, low-drama team that everyone can get behind. I'm standing behind this lineup and voting to approve it. The rest is up to the table.

Replacing Leo with Sam does not address the reason I objected: Kenji's proposal explicitly described Noah as his Evil teammate and his own place on the team as cover. His denial and later explanation have not resolved that. I will reject Kenji and Sam as well; Sam's role is still unproven, but my objection is to including Kenji.

I am on the revised team, so let me be transparent about what I know and what I don't. I am a Loyal Servant. I have no private role information, no sight of any special roles, and no evidence about anyone else's alignment. Anyone who expects me to vouch for Sam or Leo based on secret knowledge is mistaken — I have none. My vote has to rest on the public record, and on that basis I approve the revised team of Kenji and Sam.

On the public record, the substantive objection to this proposal was never about Sam at all. It was about Kenji's published draft, which described Noah as "my Evil teammate" and framed his own seat as "cover." The explanation offered was that this was scratch phrasing left in a public proposal. I want to be fair here: that explanation is plausible, and a proposal note is not a role claim, and I am not going to treat it as a confession that Kenji is Evil. But I also think the table was right to push on it, and right that the leader withdrew it and rebuilt a team instead of doubling down. Publishing something like that and then revising under pressure is not proof of anything — it is a reason to insist on plain, checkable reasoning from now on, which is exactly what Leo asked for.

That is where I part company with Maya. Maya says her objection is to including Kenji at all, yet Sam has been named as the alternative with the explicit admission that there is no evidence about Sam either. If the standard is "no unproven players," then Maya's own alternative fails it. An unproven player is not the same as an accused one, and the team has to include someone the leader does not yet have a read on — that is simply what Mission 1 looks like with five players.

So: I approve Kenji and Sam. Leo, you set a specific standard — a plain, verifiable reason, explained without cover-based positioning. Do you consider this revised team to meet that standard, given that the draft language you objected to is no longer part of the proposal and no one has raised a single concrete concern about Sam? I would like a straight answer on that point before the vote, because it is the only question left on the table.

Sam, a straight answer: no, I do not consider the revised Kenji and Sam team to meet that standard, and I will be rejecting it. The draft was not just scratch phrasing. It named Noah as Kenji's Evil teammate and presented Kenji's own seat as cover. Withdrawing that draft and swapping Leo for Sam does not change who is leading or who is on the team. Kenji is still the leader, still the person whose published reasoning we cannot verify, and still asking us to approve a team built around his own safety. Sam, I am not saying you are Evil, and I accept that you have no role information. My objection is to Kenji's presence on any team he leads. Plain, checkable reasoning going forward means a leader who is not under suspicion for a claim about a teammate. I would ask that the next proposal come from someone else.

Second turn for me, and my position has not moved, so let me state it plainly and then put one question to Leo.

I am a Loyal Servant. I have no special role information, I see no evil, and I have no private evidence about anyone at this table. Anyone who wants me to confirm or deny a role is asking the wrong person. My votes must rest on the public record.

On the public record: Kenji's original draft of the proposal named Noah as his "Evil teammate" and framed his own seat on the team as "cover." That language is the single substantive problem in this discussion, and it was never resolved by explanation — it was only withdrawn. That is not proof that Kenji is Evil, and I have not treated it as proof. But Leo's standard was reasonable: plain, checkable reasoning, and a leader who is not standing on a claim about a teammate that nobody can verify. A draft note you publish is a claim you have to live with or drop, and Kenji dropped it.

So: I reject the original team of Kenji and Leo — the cover-based reasoning behind that seat was wrong and Leo was right to say so. I approve the revised team of Kenji and Sam. Sam has been named as an alternative while admitting no one has evidence about Sam; that is not a disqualification, it is simply the state of Mission 1. The revised team also drops the draft language, which is the only concrete objection anyone raised, and no one has produced a single reason to think Sam would submit a Fail card.

My one remaining question is for Leo, and I am asking him directly because his objection now concerns the leader rather than any individual member: Leo, if the draft language is gone and Sam is on the team instead of you, are you still rejecting this team solely because Kenji leads it? If so, I want to know what specifically you believe Kenji will do on Mission 1 that a plain, checkable reason would not cover — because on the public record I can find nothing, and Maya's own alternative fails the same "unproven player" standard she applies to Sam.

I blame Kenji for the drafting, not for his role. I approve the revised team of Kenji and Sam, and I am not asking anyone to approve a team on my word — I have none to give.

Sam, to answer directly: yes, my objection is to Kenji leading this team, and it is not only about the draft wording. The draft is the only public evidence we have of Kenji's reasoning, and it tied a claim about a teammate to his own seat as cover. Withdrawing it does not tell us how he actually reasons about Mission 1. I am not claiming Kenji will fail a mission, and I have no proof of any card he will play. My point is that the public record gives us no checkable reason to trust his judgment as leader, and a leader whose own explanation was built around his safety should step back for this proposal. You asked what Kenji would do that a plain reason would not cover. My honest answer is that I cannot know, and that uncertainty is exactly why the leader should change. Sam, I am not saying you are Evil. Maya's alternative with you is also unproven, so I would prefer a fresh proposal from someone without this history. I am rejecting Kenji and Sam.

Noah, I have one specific question for you, and I would like you to answer it before the vote.

Third and final turn for me, so let me put my position on the record plainly. I am a Loyal Servant. I have no role information, I see no evil, and I have no private evidence about anyone at this table. I will not pretend otherwise, and nobody should vote on my word about anyone else.

On the public record, the only concrete objection anyone has raised in this discussion is Kenji's published draft, which named Noah as "my Evil teammate" and framed Kenji's own seat as "cover." I have said and I say again that this reasoning is wrong — a leader who justifies his seat by pointing at an alleged teammate cannot be checked. But it was withdrawn, not defended, and no one has produced a single specific reason to think Sam or Kenji would submit a Fail card on Mission 1.

So my vote is unambiguous: if the team on the table is the revised Kenji and Sam, I approve it. If the original Kenji and Leo stands, I reject it, because that seat was justified by cover-based reasoning and nothing else. Sam has been named as an alternative while admitting no one has evidence about Sam — that is not a disqualification, it is simply the state of Mission 1 with five players. A two-person team must contain someone unproven, so Maya's alternative fails her own standard, and rejecting on that basis rejects every possible team.

Noah, my question is specific: is your rejection based only on the draft language Kenji withdrew, or on anything you actually know about how Kenji or Sam will play this mission? If the latter, state it, because I would want that reason in the record before the vote rather than after. If it is only the draft language, then note that the draft language is gone, the leader rebuilt the team instead of doubling down, and rejection now buys nothing except a change of leader — which is not a neutral act when the objection on record was to wording, not to any player's play.

Sam, to answer you directly: of course I do not have private knowledge of what cards you or Kenji will play on Mission 1. I have no secret sight, so I rely entirely on what happens in public discussion. But treating Kenji's draft as merely 'wording' that can be washed away by swapping Leo for you fundamentally misses the point.

On Mission 1, before any mission cards have been cast, a player's published proposals and articulated logic are the only behavioral evidence we possess. Kenji didn't make a simple typo; his published reasoning explicitly outlined a strategy of using team placement to provide cover while framing another player. Whether that was an accidental revelation of an Evil mindset or a bizarrely reckless ploy, you cannot simply erase that context by withdrawing the note and putting you on the team instead. Kenji is still the leader, and Kenji is still putting himself on the mission.

Rejecting this team to pass leadership to Leo is not a disruptive or arbitrary act—it gives the table an opportunity to reset under a leader who hasn't compromised their credibility before the very first mission. I will not endorse a team that includes Kenji after he attempted to drag my name into his positioning. My vote remains a reject on Kenji and Sam, and I look forward to seeing a clean proposal from Leo next.

Kenji revises the team to Sam, Noah. I'm stepping off the team entirely. Sam and Noah are the two players with no concrete case against them: Sam has run his votes off the public record with care, and Noah has spent this whole discussion demanding clean, checkable reasoning with no Kenji on the mission. This proposal gives the table exactly that — no leader covering his own seat, no disputed draft language, just two players nobody has argued would submit a Fail card. I approve Sam and Noah and I'd ask the table to judge the team, not my history.
Team approved (3 approve, 2 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Leo proposes Leo, Maya, Sam. Noah and Kenji are the two Evil players I know of, so I'm leaving both off. Maya has consistently pushed against Kenji's cover-based reasoning, and Sam has no public record of sabotage. Leo, Maya, and Sam make a team with no known Evil members.

I favor Leo, Maya, and Sam over a team including Kenji. Kenji’s original proposal and subsequent denial remain strong reasons for suspicion. Mission 1’s success is encouraging for Sam and Noah, but it does not clear either of them: an Evil player can submit Success.

Leo’s statement that Noah and Kenji are Evil is stronger than what I can establish from the public record. I have no private role information, but I will approve this team based on the available evidence.

Leo, I have to strongly challenge your reasoning here. Mission 1 succeeded with Sam and myself on the team. I voted to approve that team, went on the mission, and it passed with zero fail cards.

You state that Kenji and I are 'the two Evil players I know of,' treating Kenji's bizarre smear from Mission 1 as established fact—even though I immediately denounced it and demonstrated my loyalty by delivering a clean mission. Meanwhile, you take Sam from that exact same successful mission and put him on your team, while freezing me out based entirely on Kenji's discredited words. Maya rightly noted that your certainty goes far beyond anything in the public record.

Leo, what is your concrete justification for treating Kenji's smear as proof against me, while clearing Sam when we were both on the mission that succeeded?

Noah, fair challenge, and I'll answer directly. I am not treating Kenji's draft as proof against you, and I should not have stated my Mission 2 reasoning as flatly as I did. My concern is the public record: Kenji's published draft named you as his Evil teammate, and nobody has explained that claim away. Mission 1 succeeding does not clear anyone, since an Evil player can submit Success, and Sam and Noah were both on that team. I am not clearing Sam on that basis either. My team choice rests on the public record, and I will not claim more certainty than that. Noah, you argued that any team with Kenji leading was disqualifying and called his draft a reason to reject. Then you approved Sam and Noah as soon as Kenji proposed it from off the team. What changed in your reasoning?

Leo, to answer your question directly: my standard never changed. My objection on Mission 1 was that Kenji put himself on the team to provide 'cover' after writing that absurd draft. When Kenji completely stepped aside and proposed Sam and me, the conflict of interest disappeared. I know my own alignment, Sam was unblemished, and Kenji was not on the roster. Any Good player who knows they are Good and sees the suspect leader remove himself would vote to approve a team with themselves and an untarnished player. We ran that mission, and it succeeded with zero fail cards. Now, on Mission 2, you propose Leo, Maya, and Sam, explicitly declaring: 'Noah and Kenji are the two Evil players I know of.' You walked that back as an overstatement when called out, but your proposal still isolates me while taking Sam, despite both of us delivering Mission 1. You claim to rely strictly on the public record, yet you treat Kenji's discredited smear as truth against me while handing Maya a seat without any track record. Leo, if you genuinely possess no private role information and rely solely on public evidence, why do you trust Maya over a member of the successful Mission 1 team?

Noah, you asked why I trust Maya over you. I am not ranking Maya above you on any private basis. I am weighing the public record. Maya was the first to object to the cover problem in Kenji's draft, and she has kept that same objection consistent since Mission 1. Your record is harder to square. You called a Kenji-led team disqualifying and said you would reject any team with him on it. Then Kenji stepped off the roster, proposed Sam and you, and you approved it while still calling his draft a smear. I can see that shift in your standard, but the record does not explain it. Sam's Mission 1 success does not clear him, and it does not clear you either. A successful mission only shows that the Fail cards stayed hidden, and that holds for everyone on that team. Noah, on what public basis did you accept a team that Kenji proposed after you had called him disqualifying?

Leo, to answer your question plainly: I accepted the team because of who was on the roster, not who held the leader token. A proposal is just a mechanism to get names onto a ballot; the actual game risk is entirely about who steps onto the mission. My objection was never that Kenji was holding the gavel—it was that Kenji put himself on the team under the guise of 'cover' while leveling smears. When Kenji completely stepped off, the mission became Sam and myself. From my perspective, I know with absolute certainty that I am Good, and Sam was unblemished—in fact, Sam was Maya's own proposed partner. Any Good player who sees a suspect leader step aside and hand them a mission alongside a clean player would approve it; rejecting yourself from a two-person mission when you know your own alignment makes zero tactical sense. That trust was rewarded: Mission 1 passed cleanly with zero fails.

Now, Leo, you have built a team that isolates me while keeping Sam, based on an opening draft where you claimed Kenji and I are the 'two Evil players I know of.' You walked that back when pressed, but your team still reflects that exact prejudice, preferring Maya—who has never been on a mission—over the player who helped secure our first victory.

Sam, you and I were on Mission 1 together and delivered a clean success. Leo now asks you to endorse his team, freeze me out, and trust Maya based on a narrative that Kenji's discredited Mission 1 note somehow implicates me. As a fellow Loyal Servant relying strictly on public results, do you genuinely believe it makes sense to discard the partner who just passed Mission 1 with you in favor of an untested lineup built on claims Leo admitted he cannot substantiate?

Noah asked me directly, so I will answer directly. Noah, I do not genuinely believe that Mission 1's success is a reason to trust you over Maya, and I want to be honest that Leo's framing has a real problem: he treats Kenji's withdrawn draft as truth against you while asking Sam to treat Mission 1 as proof of nothing. That is not symmetric. A mission success shows only that the Fail cards stayed hidden, and Leo said so himself. If that logic is applied honestly, it neither indicts you nor clears Sam — it simply leaves every player unproven, which is the normal state of Mission 1 and Mission 2.

On the public record, then: there is no specific reason anyone has produced to think Maya would submit a Fail card, and none to think Sam would. Leo's proposal names Noah and Kenji as "the two Evil players I know of," but he walked that back as an overstatement and said he would not claim more certainty than the public record supports. I have no private role information, I see no evil, and I have no evidence about anyone at this table, so I judge only what is said here. The only document in play is Kenji's draft, and a withdrawn draft that a player wrote about another player is not a checkable fact. Either it was accurate or it was a smear, and nobody has shown which, and Kenji's own explanation was that it was leftover scratch phrasing.

That said, I will not pretend my objection is to Noah's presence on missions. I approve the team of Leo, Maya, and Sam. I am not endorsing a veto on any player, and I am not asking anyone to vote on my word, because I have none to give. My vote rests on the absence of any concrete allegation against Leo, Maya, or Sam, and on the fact that we need three players on a five-player table, which means unproven players are unavoidable.

Leo, one specific question, because it is the only issue left: now that you have conceded that naming Kenji and Noah as known Evil players goes beyond what the public record supports, will you restate your reasoning for including Maya without that claim — and will you accept that if the only ground for excluding Noah is a discredited draft, then the same standard should mean I am not cleared by Mission 1 either? I would like your answer before the vote, not after it.

Sam, fair question, and I'll answer it directly. I agree with your symmetry point: Mission 1 succeeding clears nobody, including Sam and Noah, and I am not treating it as proof for or against anyone. I should have stated my Mission 2 reasoning more carefully, and I withdraw the claim that Noah and Kenji are the two Evil players I know of. My restated reasoning for this team rests only on the public record. Kenji's published draft said Noah was his Evil teammate and framed his own seat as cover, and that draft has never been explained beyond 'scratch phrasing.' Kenji's public reasoning is the core problem, so I have kept him off this mission. Maya is the only player who objected to that draft from the first proposal and has kept the same objection consistent through every round. I can check that against the record. Noah's position has shifted: he called a Kenji-led team disqualifying, then approved a Sam and Noah team that Kenji proposed after stepping off, and he defends that by saying the roster changed rather than the reasoning. I can see that shift, even if I cannot prove it is wrong. So for this vote, the comparison is simple: Maya's record on the draft is consistent, and Noah's is not. On your standard, I accept it. If the only ground for excluding Noah were the draft, then Sam would also be uncleared by Mission 1. That is why this team is a choice about who has the cleaner public record, not a claim of proof about Sam. Given that, I think the public record supports Leo, Maya, and Sam over Kenji's proposed team.

Leo's revised reasoning is much cleaner than his opening draft, and I'll approve Leo, Maya, and Sam. Leo walked back the overstatement about Noah and me, which is exactly what I asked of him earlier — state your case on the public record without claiming more than you can show. What remains is straightforward: Maya has been consistent from Mission 1 onward in objecting to my draft language, Sam has been careful and transparent about having no private information, and Leo has shown no reason to play a Fail card. All three are reasonable choices for a three-player mission.

I also want to be clear about where I stand on the record. I was the leader whose published draft caused this entire discussion, and I accept that it was a mistake. I stepped off the team in Mission 1 precisely because the table deserved a leader whose reasoning was not built around his own seat. Leo's Mission 2 proposal does the same thing — it puts three players forward with plain reasoning and no one claiming special knowledge.

I approve this team.

Second turn for me on this proposal, and my position has not moved. I approve the team of Leo, Maya, and Sam.

Let me be transparent again, because I have nothing else to offer. I am a Loyal Servant. I have no special role information, I see no evil, and I have no private evidence about anyone at this table, so I am not asking anyone to vote on my word about anyone else. My vote rests entirely on the public record, and it is a vote on the absence of concrete allegations rather than on proof of anything.

On the record as it now stands: Leo has withdrawn his claim that Noah and Kenji are "the two Evil players I know of," and his restated reasoning is narrower and more honest. He says Kenji stays off because Kenji's published draft has never been explained beyond scratch phrasing, and Maya gets a seat because her objection to that draft has been consistent from the first proposal onward. Both of those are statements about what is visible in the record, and both of them are checkable. Leo has also accepted Sam's symmetry point, that Mission 1's success clears nobody, and that this is a choice about who has the cleaner public record rather than a claim of proof about Sam. I agree with that framing and I am not going to pretend otherwise.

What I will not do is treat a withdrawn draft as a fact. Kenji's Mission 1 note said something that reads like a confession; it was never substantiated, it was never defended, and Kenji said it was leftover drafting language. Either it was accurate or it was a smear, and nobody has shown which. That uncertainty belongs to Kenji, and Leo is right to keep him off a mission he leads. It does not transfer into evidence against Noah, and I say that plainly because Noah has made exactly this argument and he is right on it.

Maya, I have one specific question for you, and I want a direct answer before the vote rather than after it: your stated reason for rejecting Kenji's teams on Mission 1 was the published draft and the cover-based reasoning attached to his own seat. You have said the same thing again here about Kenji. But Leo's current proposal does not include Kenji at all, and Leo's reason for excluding Noah is that Noah's own position shifted when he approved a Kenji-proposed roster after calling Kenji disqualifying. My question is this: do you think Noah's shift is genuine evidence of something, or are you treating it as equivalent to Kenji's draft note? If it is the latter, then on your own Mission 1 standard you would have to treat the draft as a smear too, and that would put Kenji back in the pool and change the shape of this mission. I would like your answer, because it is the last question that actually affects how I read this vote.

Sam, I do not consider Noah’s approval of Sam and Noah a meaningful shift: he objected to Kenji being on the mission, and Kenji stepped off. Nor do I treat that decision as equivalent to Kenji’s draft. The draft remains a strong reason to suspect Kenji, but it does not establish Noah’s alignment.

Mission 1’s success clears neither Sam nor Noah. I know I am Good, and I have no private information about anyone else. I still favor and will approve Leo, Maya, and Sam, while recognizing that Leo and Sam are unproven.

My position has not changed: I approve Leo, Maya, Sam for Mission 2.

Leo's restated reasoning is grounded in the record — he withdrew the overstatement about Noah and me, and his team choice rests on Maya's consistent record and the absence of concrete allegations against any of the three. Sam has been transparent about having no private information, and I have found nothing in the public record to suggest any of these three would submit a Fail card.

I do want to put something on the record for future rounds. Noah delivered on Mission 1 alongside Sam, and that mission passed with zero fails. Maya herself has acknowledged that Noah's approval of the Sam-Noah team does not establish his alignment. The draft language that has driven suspicion of Noah was never substantiated and was withdrawn. I am not asking anyone to change their vote on this mission — I approve this team — but when Mission 3 arrives, I would ask the table to weigh Noah's actual mission performance alongside the draft note, because a document is not a play, and the only behavioral evidence anyone has produced so far is that clean Mission 1 result.

Third and final turn for me on this proposal, so let me put my position on the record without repeating myself.

I approve the team of Leo, Maya, and Sam. I have no private role information, I see no evil, and I have no evidence about anyone at this table, so my vote rests entirely on the public record and on the absence of concrete allegations.

Let me be precise about what that record does and does not say. It does not say anything about Maya, and it does not say anything about Sam, and it does not say anything about Leo beyond the fact that he withdrew his original overstatement about Kenji and Noah and restated his reasoning in terms he can actually check. What the record does say is that Kenji's Mission 1 draft remains unexplained, and Leo's choice to keep Kenji off a mission Leo leads is a coherent response to that. I support it.

What the record does not do is convert that unexplained draft into evidence against Noah. Leo has accepted that, Maya has accepted that, and I think the table should record it plainly: the draft belongs to Kenji, and its uncertainty stays with Kenji. Mission 1's success clears nobody either, which means we are approving this team on consistency of public reasoning rather than on proof of anyone's alignment. That is exactly the state of play on Mission 2 with five players and a three-person team, and unproven players are unavoidable. Rejecting on that ground rejects every possible team, and the fifth rejection on one mission would hand Evil the game outright.

One thing I want on the record for the rest of the game: Kenji's Mission 1 note is a document, not a play. The only behavioral evidence any of us has seen so far is two team missions passing cleanly. As we go to Mission 3, the standard should be what each of us actually does on the table, and nobody's alignment should be treated as established by a withdrawn line of draft text.

Maya, one specific question, because you have been the most consistent voice at this table and I want this settled before the vote rather than after it: do you commit that on Mission 3, absent new evidence, you will not treat Kenji's Mission 1 draft as evidence against Noah, and that you will judge Noah only on what he does and says going forward? A yes from you closes the remaining gap between your Mission 1 standard and your Mission 2 standard, and I would like it on the record.

Sam, I will not treat Kenji’s draft as proof of Noah’s alignment. I will consider all available evidence, including what Noah says and does, without committing in advance to ignore the draft entirely.

Also, only Mission 1 has been completed; Mission 2 has not yet been voted on or played. I still approve Leo, Maya, and Sam, though neither Leo nor Sam is cleared.

Leo confirms Leo, Maya, Sam. I'm keeping Leo, Maya, and Sam. Kenji's Mission 1 draft is still unexplained and I'd rather not put him on this mission. Maya has been consistent in her objections to that draft, and Sam has made no concrete allegations and has been transparent about having no role information. Mission 1 succeeding clears nobody, so this comes down to who has the cleaner public record.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 2 succeeds (0 fail cards).
Maya proposes Maya, Leo. I know I am Good. Leo’s team succeeded on Mission 2, and he has consistently kept Kenji off the mission, though the success does not prove Leo’s alignment.

Maya, I want to make a direct case for Noah's inclusion on this Mission 3 team.

Noah has the strongest mission record at this table. He was on the clean Mission 1 team with Sam, delivered zero fail cards, and was then excluded from Mission 2 based on reasoning Leo himself withdrew as an overstatement. You, Maya, have said repeatedly that my draft does not prove Noah's alignment — you committed to not treating it as proof against him going forward. I take you at your word.

So the question is simple: what public evidence justifies keeping Noah off this team? The only document in play is my withdrawn draft, and you have already conceded it does not condemn Noah. His actual behavior shows a clean mission and consistent public reasoning. Two missions have succeeded without him, and each time the table has leaned on my drafting rather than on anything he has done.

A team of Maya and Leo is defensible on the record, but it repeats the pattern of Mission 2: freeze Noah out based on a note he had nothing to do with, then carry on. I am asking you to consider a revision that brings Noah in. If you do not think that is warranted, I would like to hear the specific reason before the vote.

Kenji, I am not excluding Noah simply because of your draft. I know I am Good, and Leo was on the successful Mission 2 team with me. Noah’s successful Mission 1 is encouraging, but an Evil player could have played Success on either mission, so neither result clears anyone. Your original draft and subsequent denial remain reasons to be cautious about your recommendations, too.

Maya and Leo is not proven safe, but I see no reason to replace Leo with Noah on the evidence available. I favor keeping the proposed team.

Maya, I hear you, and I'm not going to relitigate my draft for the third time. You've said it doesn't prove Noah's alignment, and I take that at face value. My question is narrower.

The team you've proposed is Maya and Leo. Leo delivered on Mission 2 alongside you, and I'm not disputing that. rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
